summary: Describes a method for compressing the IP, UDP and RTP headers of audio and video packets to cut overhead on low-speed serial links. Because these headers are large compared with small voice packets, compressing them makes better use of limited bandwidth.

plainLanguage.summary: Audio and video packets can be small while their IP, UDP and RTP headers are relatively large. This RFC describes a link-by-link method for compressing those headers while preserving the original packet information.

questions: how small does crtp make ip udp rtp headers
what is a compression context id
subtitle: How a point-to-point link compresses IP, UDP and RTP headers for real-time media.

tldr.problem: IP, UDP and RTP headers can use more bandwidth than small audio payloads on low-speed links such as dial-up modems.
tldr.mechanism: The compressor and decompressor keep shared state for each stream and encode only fields that change. RTP fields with predictable increments can be reconstructed from the previous header.
tldr.outcome: The combined headers can often shrink to 2 bytes without UDP checksums or 4 bytes with them. The method includes feedback to recover when packet loss leaves contexts out of sync.

facts.label: Compressed header
facts.value: 2 bytes without UDP checksum; 4 with checksum

today: RFC 2508 is a Proposed Standard published in February 1999. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is designed to fit the IP header-compression framework in RFC 2507.

sections.title: The Header Overhead Problem
sections.content:
Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) carries audio and video. Its 12-byte header is significant overhead when a packet carries a 20-byte payload over a 14.4 or 28.8 kb/s dial-up modem.

RFC 2508 compresses the combined IP, UDP and RTP headers one link at a time. The combined headers can be 40 bytes, yet the compressed result is typically 2 to 4 bytes. The method can be used with IPv4, IPv6 and packets with multiple IP headers, though the initial focus is IPv4.

The scheme fits within the broader IP header-compression framework of RFC 2507 and builds on the TCP/IP compression design in RFC 1144.
sections.plainLanguage: For small media packets on slow links, the headers use a large share of the transmission capacity. This method compresses the IP, UDP and RTP headers together.

sections.title: Assumptions and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The target is audio and video over low-speed links, including 14.4 and 28.8 kb/s modems. The scheme works best on local links with low round-trip time and uses a return path to report compression errors quickly. It can also operate over simplex links, but recovery is slower there.

The specification addresses compression, not segmentation of large packets. A separate layer may segment large packets so small real-time packets can be sent between them. The link layer must identify packet types, provide packet lengths and detect errors reliably.

The RFC compresses IP, UDP and RTP together because compressing only RTP gives less benefit, while the resulting header is about the same size.
sections.plainLanguage: The method works best when the link supports traffic in both directions and has low delay. It compresses headers only; another layer can handle packet segmentation if needed.

sections.title: Shared Session Context
sections.content:
The compressor and decompressor keep a shared context for each stream. A session context is identified by the IP source and destination addresses, UDP source and destination ports, and the RTP SSRC field. A Context Identifier (CID) tells the decompressor which stored context to use.

Many RTP fields change predictably. For example, the RTP sequence number often increases by one and audio timestamps often increase by a constant amount. When the second-order difference is zero, the receiver can reconstruct the next values from the previous header and stored increments.

RTP compression is lossless and can be attempted on UDP streams. If a stream does not behave like RTP, the compressor may continue with IP and UDP compression alone.
sections.plainLanguage: The two endpoints store the previous headers and predictable changes for each stream. The CID selects that stored information so the receiver can rebuild the current header.

sections.title: Packet Types and Compressed RTP Fields
sections.content:
The link layer distinguishes FULL_HEADER, COMPRESSED_UDP, COMPRESSED_RTP and CONTEXT_STATE packets, in addition to ordinary IP packets. A full header initializes the context. COMPRESSED_UDP compresses IP and UDP but leaves the RTP header uncompressed. COMPRESSED_RTP compresses all three headers when the expected field changes can be inferred.

Each packet carries a CID and a 4-bit sequence number for detecting loss. A compressed RTP header includes a flag mask for changes such as the IPv4 packet ID, RTP marker, sequence number and timestamp. A nonzero UDP checksum is sent in each compressed packet. If other fixed RTP fields change, the sender sends an uncompressed RTP header.

With IPv6, implementations may also use COMPRESSED_NON_TCP from RFC 2507. Numeric PPP codes for the packet types are assigned by IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: A full header establishes state; later packet types carry only compressed IP and UDP data, or compressed IP, UDP and RTP data. A sequence number helps detect when a packet was lost.

sections.title: Encoding Changes Between Packets
sections.content:
When a header field changes, the compressor encodes the difference rather than repeating the whole value. The default encoding uses one byte for changes from 0 through 127, and uses two or three bytes for larger values. The RFC recommends a table-driven encoder and decoder so a link can use a table suited to its traffic.

Negative changes can occur when packets are reordered or video timestamps move backward. If an RTP timestamp change is below -16384 or above 4194303, the RTP header must be sent uncompressed. The protocol keeps IP, UDP and RTP data intact when it reconstructs the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Small changes use short encodings, while larger changes use more bytes. If a timestamp change is outside the supported range, the sender sends the RTP header without compression.

sections.title: Detecting Loss and Restoring Context
sections.content:
Each context has its own 4-bit link sequence number. If the decompressor sees a sequence number that does not follow the previous one, it invalidates the context and sends a CONTEXT_STATE packet to the compressor. It discards packets for that context until a full refresh arrives.

The compressor may retransmit CONTEXT_STATE information if it may have been lost. When UDP checksums are sent, the decompressor may try the twice algorithm from RFC 2507, applying a change more than once and checking whether the checksum matches. Because a false match is possible, the RFC recommends checking UDP checksums periodically.
sections.plainLanguage: A sequence-number gap tells the receiver that context may be wrong. The receiver can request a full header and ignore that stream until the compressor restores the context.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encryption hides the repeated patterns that compression uses. The RFC notes that this may create pressure to avoid encryption on a slow link. RTP can instead encrypt only the payload in cases where that protection is acceptable, leaving headers available for compression.

A faulty or malicious compressor could cause the decompressor to reconstruct different packets that still have valid-looking headers. End-to-end authentication and integrity checks can detect such corruption. CONTEXT_STATE packets are not authenticated, so an attacker able to inject packets on the link could reduce compression efficiency, though the RFC notes that such an attacker can disrupt traffic in other ways too.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression does not provide message security, and encryption can remove the patterns that compression uses. End-to-end integrity checks can detect packets that were reconstructed incorrectly.
